v.why: Adding a direct skip where there was none gives a large gain in gradient flow and accuracy.
Even a pooling op on an empty direct edge adds a path, which beats replacing an existing op.
Replacing the helpful skip with a conv gives little gain or a loss, compared with filling an empty edge.
Removing a 3x3 conv on the input edge loses a lot more than removing a weak op.
The skip's benefit shrinks when a strong conv path to the output already exists.
A strong conv path into the output reduces the marginal value of a direct skip.
Without edge 1, node 2 is fed only via the longer route through nodes 0 and 1, so edge 5 matters less.
With edge 4 removed, node 1 only reaches the output via edges 2 and 5, so edge 0 matters less.
Adding a conv onto an empty output edge gains more than replacing a non-empty op.
Filling an empty edge with a 3x3 conv gains more than a swap.

raw:
These are the 10 I rate at 55% or higher. Most of the candidates I dropped are obvious from graph structure alone, such as an edit on a dead branch or a no-op edit. The reasoning I expect to mislead other raters is that a weaker op, or one that duplicates an existing path, is "not meaningful". The comparison actually runs against replacing existing ops, which often lowers accuracy, so filling an empty edge looks relatively better.
